How it spreadA TIMELINE, FEBRUARY TO JULY 2026
EARLY FEB 2026

The journal appears

Its founder, Woniu Xuezhang (“Snail Senior”), launches S.H.I.T. Journal and calls it a “shelter for academic garbage.”

MID-FEB TO EARLY MAR 2026

It quickly goes viral

Absurd academic papers spread widely on social media and draw in users from outside academia.

BY 7 MAR 2026
100M+

views in about a month

News reports say that about a month after launch, related topics had passed 100 million views in total.

MID-MAR 2026

Platform limits and controversy

Some accounts, content and videos were deleted or restricted, and much of the original material disappeared.

AFTER MAR 2026

It spreads on, and adjusts

The journal keeps going through its website and other channels, and a discussion of changes to its name and form appears.

APR TO JUL 2026

What came next

People laugh together. The joke is a way to say something heavy without sounding too heavy.

Second, people recognize themselves. “This is my life” is probably the most common sentence in the comments.

Third, people start to talk about the journal itself. Is it useful? Should it be allowed to exist? And when the platform limits it, people talk about that too. A restriction becomes a topic. Sometimes even a reason to defend it.

I read the comments like a very patient neighbor who can hear everything through the wall. I don’t know the whole thing. But I can tell you what the group is saying out loud.

SCRIPT

But I couldn’t stop thinking about it. So I want to take you back about a hundred and ten years. Imagine China around 1915.

At that time, serious writing was done in classical Chinese. It was a very old, very formal style. Most ordinary people couldn’t read it easily. It’s as if, today, every text message had to be written like Shakespeare. “Shall I compare thee to a summer’s day.” (pause) Not very practical.

SCRIPT

Then a magazine appeared. It was called New Youth. Its message was simple, and, for that time, shocking. It said: Write the way you speak. Question old authority. Don’t accept an idea just because it’s old. Let science and democracy into the conversation.

You can think of New Youth as a group chat for young people who felt that the old rules were no longer working. And the group chat got very loud. It started what we now call the New Culture Movement.

TIP

The cover at the top right is a real New Youth cover (Volume 2, Issue 5), shown whole. The big NEW YOUTH type on the left is stretched vertically on purpose. The four faces are stylized illustrations of people connected to the magazine, not portraits: Chen Duxiu (founder, 1915), Hu Shi (a key voice for literary reform), Li Dazhao (a major contributor), and Lu Xun (the story on the next slide). I can merge the next slide into this one if you prefer, or swap in real portraits if you send them.

RESEARCH QUESTION 2

How do users use the New Culture Movement to understand what this journal means?

SCRIPT

Now you might see why some people made that comparison. S.H.I.T. Journal also plays with the same question: Who gets to speak in academic language? Who decides what counts as serious knowledge? And what happens when ordinary people laugh at it?

But I need to clarify that I am not saying S.H.I.T. Journal is the new New Youth. Big claims need big evidence. I have a laptop and some patience. My question is smaller, and more honest: how do users make this connection? And what do they mean when they do?

Maybe it’s a joke. Maybe a very proud joke. Maybe a serious comparison. Maybe it’s both at the same time, which is very common on the internet.

And the answer tells us something. Because when people choose a historical story to explain a joke journal, they’re also telling us how they see academic authority, how knowledge is made, and who gets to speak.

That’s my second research question: how do users use the New Culture Movement to understand what this journal means?

SCRIPT

So where am I now? I’m still early. Now I collect public videos and comments by hand, and read them carefully. So far, I have about sixty videos and over six hundred comments. I use a software called NVivo to organize them.

And I’ll be honest. I don’t have final answers yet. What I have are patterns that keep showing up: people talk about platform limits, people talk about whether the journal has value, and people talk about shared feelings. Those are my starting points, not my conclusions.

SCRIPT

So, let’s go back to the name. A journal named after a swear word. A joke that a platform tried to limit. A comment section that turned into a group of people saying “me too.” And a hundred-year-old magazine, suddenly in the room.

When people laugh at the same thing, at the same time, they’re not only laughing. They’re telling us how they feel, who they feel close to, and what they think about the ones who decide what counts as “serious.”

My job is to listen carefully. And, in my thesis, to laugh a little less. (pause) Thank you.
